Japanese anchovy Engraulis japonicus is a small pelagic clupeiform that attains a maximum total length of 18 cm [Li = 18 cm], a size typical of coastal schooling engraulids. The standard length at which individuals first demonstrate pubertal development is 10.5 cm [Lp = 10.5 cm], indicating that reproductive maturation begins well before the cessation of somatic growth. Field surveys and laboratory rearing trials conducted at 24 °C [T = 24 °C] have established that the embryonic period, from ovum fertilisation through larval eclosion, lasts approximately 31 hours, which translates to an age at birth of approximately 1.29 days [ab = approximately 1.29 days] under those thermal conditions. This rapid developmental pace is characteristic of warm-water engraulids and contrasts with the longer incubation periods observed in cooler temperate environments.

Under the elevated thermal regime of 29.6 °C [T = 29.6 °C], the time from egg fertilisation to hatching shortens markedly, with the age at birth measured at approximately 0.85 days [ab = approximately 0.85 days], a reduction of roughly one-third compared to the duration at 24 °C [T = 24 °C]. This strong inverse relationship between temperature and embryonic development time is consistent with the metabolic acceleration typical of polkilothermic teleosts. The freshly spawned egg of Engraulis japonicus is a transparent, pelagic sphere measuring approximately 1.21 mm in length and 0.63 mm in width. From these dimensions, the wet weight at birth has been calculated at 0.00025 grams [Wwb = 0.00025 grams], a minute starting mass that underscores the species extreme fecundity and high larval mortality characteristic of small pelagic spawners.

Analysis of length-weight relationships in Engraulis japonicus indicates that the adult body mass of a fish at the ultimate total length of 18 cm [Li = 18 cm] reaches approximately 620 grams [Wwi = approximately 620 grams], representing the maximum recorded wet weight for this species. This asymptotic mass is derived from a power-law model fitted to extensive morphometric data collected from the Japan Sea stock. In tandem with this somatic growth limit, longevity records based on otolith readings from congeners suggest a maximum lifespan of 10 years [am = 10 years] at an ambient temperature of 18.4 °C [T = 18.4 °C]. Such a lifespan is relatively extended for a small clupeiform and likely reflects the seasonally pulsed, energy-conserving metabolic regime of this migratory fish.

The maximum reproductive rate of Engraulis japonicus has been estimated through comparative studies of the closely related European anchovy Engraulis encrasicolus, with the daily egg output reaching 600 eggs per day [Ri = 600 eggs per day] under optimal foraging conditions at 18.4 °C [T = 18.4 °C]. This prodigious spawning capacity is facilitated by a high-frequency batch-spawning strategy, where individual females release multiple clutches across an extended breeding season. Field surveys corroborate this rate, recording gravid individuals with hydrated oocytes throughout the summer months in the productive Kuroshio Current region. Such a high daily reproductive allocation is energetically demanding and is supported by the anchovy’s efficient filter-feeding on abundant zooplankton blooms.

Comparisons with other small pelagic clupeiforms reveal that the ultimate total length of 18 cm [Li = 18 cm] places Engraulis japonicus at the upper end of the size range for the genus, with most congeners rarely exceeding 15 cm. Similarly, the estimated maximum lifespan of 3,650 days [am = 3,650 days] at 18.4 °C [T = 18.4 °C] is notably greater than the two- to three-year longevity typical of temperate anchovy populations, a difference that may be linked to the cooler, more stable thermal environment of the Japan Sea. The embryonic development under different thermal conditions—approximately 1.29 days [ab = approximately 1.29 days] at 24 °C and approximately 0.85 days [ab = approximately 0.85 days] at 29.6 °C—reveals a pronounced thermal sensitivity that has direct implications for larval survival and recruitment success in variable coastal waters at a temperature of 24 °C [T = 24 °C] at a temperature of 24 °C [T = 24 °C].
